text:
The barometer in the foyer of my building had been falling since Tuesday, its brass needle twitching toward *Change*, though what arrived on Thursday afternoon was less a change than a slow, pressurized saturation. I was standing under the green canvas awning of a closed dry cleaner’s on Bergen Street when I first saw them. 

They were arguing, or had just finished arguing, with the exhausted choreography of people who have lived together long enough to edit out the transitions. He was tall, wearing a beige trench coat gone dark at the shoulders from the drizzle, carrying a damp paper grocery sack with leeks poking out the top. She was half a head shorter, her blonde hair darkened to the color of wet hemp and plastered to her collarbones. She wore an oversized, rust-colored cardigan that soaked up the mist rather than repelling it. 

What held me was not their negligible beauty or their standard October misery. It was the way they stopped in front of the ruin at the curb.

Someone had left an armchair beside the streetlamp. It had once been covered in a mustard-yellow cotton brocade, the sort of mid-century facsimile one buys on credit in one’s twenties, but a fire had taken the center of it. The beechwood legs were untouched, and the left rolled arm remained intact, if waterlogged. The seat and backrest, however, had been gutted by flame, leaving a crater of blackened ticking, gray ash compacted by the rain into paste, and a single coiled spring jutting upward like a snapped collarbone. The smell of wet char hung around it in a tight, greasy halo.

The man shifted the grocery sack and looked down into the crater. "How does that even happen?" he said, his voice nasal and flat. "You set the chair on fire, you get it down three flights of stairs before the curtains go?"

The woman didn't answer. She reached out with two unvarnished, bitten-down fingers and touched the wet, unburned mustard fabric of the left arm. Then she moved an inch to the right, where the cloth turned brittle and black, flaking away under her skin. She rubbed the smudge of wet soot between her thumb and forefinger as if testing the grade of a spice.

"Come on, Claire," he said, already moving. "The drains are backing up on Hoyt."

She followed him. And then, for reasons that had everything to do with my three-day headache and the stack of uncorrected galleys waiting in my fourth-floor walkup, I stepped out from under the awning and followed them too.

It is easy to trail people in bad weather; the city contracts into a series of private, hurrying capsules. I kept thirty paces behind them. As we crossed Court Street, the rain shifted gears, descending in grey, billowing sheets driven off the harbor. Municipal warnings had been chiming on phones since noon—*flash flood watch, coastal surge*—the usual liturgy of encroaching ruin. Now, the gutters were no longer gulping water; they were regurgitating it. Brown fountains bubbled up through the iron grates, carrying flattened cigarette packs, sycamore leaves, and a slick of petrol.

Claire walked through the rising puddles without altering her stride, letting the water take her ankles. Her husband—I had decided they were married, bound by some shared, unremarkable catastrophe—hopped from high curb to stoop base, protecting his loafers. At the corner of Carroll, she looked back once. I stopped beside a submerged hydrant, pretending to struggle with my ruined umbrella. Her pale, skim-milk blue eyes passed directly over my face, entirely incurious. She wasn't looking to see if she was being followed; she was looking back toward Bergen Street, as if to check whether the chair had begun to float.

They turned down a dead-end mews off President Street, where the old carriage houses sat low to the ground without stoops. The water here was already ankle-deep, pooling in the depressions of the Belgian blocks. They went into number 14, a narrow brick facade painted peeling slate gray. Two seconds later, a yellow rectangle of light appeared in the parlor window level with the street.

My trousers were soaked to the knees, my shoes leaden troughs. Instead of seeking higher ground, I waded fifteen feet into the cul-de-sac and positioned myself behind a parked Volvo wagon.

Through the horizontal slats of the wide wooden Venetian blinds, the room appeared sliced into luminous ribbons. It possessed the signifiers of warmth: dark pine bookshelves, a faded rug, a brass floor lamp casting an amber circle. The man disappeared into the rear of the house and returned without the groceries, rubbing his hair with a blue hand towel. He was talking, his jaw working rhythmically, his hands gesturing toward the ceiling and floorboards. He was discussing the water table, the sump pump, the landlord. He was a man who believed in maintenance.

Claire hadn't taken off her sodden cardigan. She stood in the center of the rug, water dripping from her skirt onto the wool, arms wrapped loosely around her ribs. 

Around my knees, the water rose with stealthy efficiency, backed up from the Gowanus Canal four blocks downhill, bringing its ancient stink of coal tar and sewage. A green recycling bin drifted lazily past my hip. 

Inside the amber box, the man approached Claire and put the blue towel over her head to dry her hair—a gesture of domestic truce, rough but affectionate. She didn't pull away. She simply stood beneath the towel, utterly inert, the black smudge from the chair still on her thumb. When he lifted the towel, her face had the flat, calcined blankness of things that have already been through the fire.

I thought of the armchair on Bergen Street. By now, the rain would be filling its charred bowl, turning the carbon into a cold slurry. What was left on the sidewalk still occupied the space of a chair; you could still name its parts. Only the place where a human body was meant to rest had been hollowed out to the springs.

In the window, whatever the man saw in her face finally interrupted his monologue. He stepped back, turned, and walked out of the room, leaving her alone.

The water was at my thighs now, frigid and oily. Across the alley, a basement window gave way with a muffled, aquatic thud, and the river swirled as it poured into the new void. 

Claire walked to the window. She didn't look down at the water lapping two inches below the sill, or out at the Volvo where I stood shivering. She leaned her forehead against the glass, her breath fogging a small oval that quickly vanished. Then she reached up, took the cord of the blind in her soot-stained fingers, and pulled. The slats snapped shut like a row of eyelids, leaving me in the rising black water, with nothing left to watch but my own hands floating on the surface.
